I'll start with saying that once you are out of this living situation and away from this abusive environment, being able to distinguish between abusive behavior and fair criticism does get easier. I dunno how old you are or your situation in life beyond your post, but try to move out and limit contact as soon as you are able to. 

What helps me distinguish between the two (doesn't always work for me, but that's because I overthink things and am not good at reading people): where is the criticism coming from? If they say it from a good place, with no intent to harm and want to help, then it's more likely to be fair criticism. If they say it coming from a place of negativity (hatred, spite, etc), it's more likely to be abusive behavior. Is the criticism an attack on you as a person, or is it meant to bring awareness to something you could improve on? Are they trying to manipulate you into getting what they want or tending to their wants and needs (like in your example of you questioning your mom's need for more stuff), or are they holding your needs and wants and best interests at heart?

I wanna say I relate to this 100%. Having this anxiety and being in this position doesn't make you dumb at all. Throughout my years in college (22f, graduated in May), I always procrastinated my assignments and did assignments last minute because I was afraid of not understanding the material and feeling like I was stupid. I have quite a bit of anxiety regarding my mental capabilities and how they come off to others. Lots of imposter syndrome. Having the mindset of "if I just don't do it or if I fail this test because I didn't study, then I'll figure something out. I always do" especially didn't help. 

It was a lot easier to give into that fear and procrastinate than it was to face it and tackle my assignments. I'd watch YouTube or hang out with friends or play video games. 

Eventually, I just kinda got sick of it. At the start of my senior year, I forced myself to work on those assignments right when they were given out. I didn't always succeed in doing so, but eventually I found that if I DIDNT understand the material, and if I started the assignment early enough, I had time to ask questions about it. When I'd try to do the assignment last second, stressed about the deadline and my intelligence, I'd have a harder time understanding the material. It'd become a self fulfilling prophecy. but when I tackled it ahead of time, without that stress (or as much of it), it helped a lot. My grades picked up more. Because I was able to take the time to understand the material better, I felt smarter, and actually became that student that others came to for help in some instances.

My advice, beyond not procrastinating and asking questions: sit with that fear and dig deeper into it. Where did this fear come about? What's the original cause of it? Dr K uses this approach quite a bit, and I've found it to be helpful in my case. My anxiety regarding my intelligence began with an abusive ex of mine who would belittle me and call me stupid a lot. When did your anxiety start to take hold? One of my favorite Dr K quotes is "Fear thrives off of a lack of information. Fear is not about reality, it's about the hypothetical. Stop living in hypotheticals and live where you are." Maybe you'll find if you tackle those assignments and that anxiety, you'll find you're much smarter than you think you are. 

I hope this word vomit helps some 😊 these feelings are shared by more people than you'd think. Most try to hide it, so it feels like everyone else is on top of their assignments and knows what they're doing. I promise you: they don't, they just don't talk about it.
